## Response

The chapter describes descriptive analysis as the “first conversation” with your data — and that metaphor captures why it’s so essential to begin every research project by fully describing your sample before you leap to hypotheses or conclusions. First, a dataset straight from collection tends to be messy, overwhelming, and uninformative — a spreadsheet full of numbers or coded responses that doesn’t yet “mean” anything. By applying descriptive statistics and data visualization, you turn that raw data into an intelligible summary of what your sample actually looks like: its central tendencies, its distribution, its variability, and potential outliers. Without doing this first step, you risk building inferences — or worse, claims — on faulty ground. For example: if your data are skewed, an average (mean) may give a misleading impression of the “typical” case; a median might be more appropriate. Or outliers could distort results in subtle ways that only become visible once you graph the distribution. Jumping straight to hypothesis testing or inferential statistics without this “first look” ignores such nuances and increases the chance you draw invalid conclusions. Moreover, descriptive analysis helps you check assumptions: Did the sample behave as you expected? Are there unexpected gaps, weird values, or unbalanced groups? This matters because statistical tests often rely on assumptions (e.g., distribution shape, homogeneity of variance). If those assumptions don’t hold, your hypothesis tests might become misleading. In short: descriptive analysis is not just a trivial preliminary — it is the foundation of integrity in research. Skipping it risks bad research: you might misrepresent what your data really show, overlook problems, or draw conclusions that simply don’t hold in the real distribution of your sample.

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
